what: Static site generation (SSG) renders every page to a plain HTML file at build time, before anyone visits. The files are copied to a CDN, so each request is just a file download.
like: Like printing a book once and putting copies on every shelf, instead of writing a fresh copy by hand for each reader.
why: Fastest, most predictable first byte - a CDN serves a file with no server work
Cheap and very resilient: no render server to scale or to fail
Content is real HTML, so search engines and link previews just work

nodes.t: HTML + JS + CSS|one file per URL

steps.d: The build pulls data from markdown, a headless CMS or an API. Whatever is not known at build time cannot be in the page.
The build runs your components once per URL and writes an HTML file for each. Dynamic routes need a list of params, such as generateStaticParams in Next.js.
The output folder (for example out/ in a Next.js static export) can be hosted by any server that serves static files, with hashed assets cached long-term.
Each request is a cache hit at the nearest edge, so TTFB is low and consistent however many users arrive.
Ship little JS: only components that must be interactive hydrate. Personalised parts load from APIs on the client after the static shell.

numbers.l: rough 'good' TTFB threshold; static files from a CDN usually sit well inside it
what a Next.js static export emits per route (index.html, blog/post-1.html and so on)
good LCP threshold at the 75th percentile

choices.d: Rarely (docs, marketing, blog): SSG is ideal. Every few minutes or per user: use ISR, SSR or client fetches instead. web.dev notes SSG must generate a file for every URL, which is hard for very large or unpredictable sites.

choices.t: Build time vs number of pages
choices.d: Build time grows with page count. Pre-render the popular pages and generate the long tail on demand (ISR) rather than building millions of files.
Keep the shell static and fetch personal or fast-changing data on the client, or use server islands. This keeps the page cacheable.
A pure export hosts anywhere but drops features that need a server, such as cookies, redirects, rewrites, ISR and default image optimisation.

instead.why: Same static speed, but pages refresh in the background without a full rebuild
Highly interactive private app where per-user content dominates

breaks.d: Pages only change when you rebuild and redeploy.
breaks.see: Editors say their change is not live
breaks.fix: Trigger a rebuild from CMS webhooks, or move that route to ISR with on-demand revalidation

breaks.d: Tens of thousands of routes rendered on every deploy.
breaks.fix: Prebuild top pages only, generate the rest on first request, cache build output between runs

breaks.d: Server-only features used with output: export.
breaks.fix: Drop to a hosted runtime or move the logic to an API or edge function

say: For content that changes slowly I would statically generate the pages at build time and serve them from a CDN - fastest and cheapest option, and great for SEO.
Personalised or fast-changing bits are fetched on the client after the static shell, so the page itself stays cacheable.
If the site is huge or editors need quick updates, I move to ISR rather than rebuilding everything on each change.

followups.q: How do you handle a page that needs the logged-in user's name?
followups.a: Serve the static shell, then fetch the user on the client or use a deferred server island, so the HTML stays cacheable for everyone.

Static rendering produces real per-URL HTML at build time. web.dev distinguishes it from prerendering a client app, which captures initial state as HTML but still needs client JS to become interactive.

today: Static-first frameworks lean on partial JavaScript: Astro ships zero JS by default and adds interactive islands, and Next.js static exports now include Server Components rendered at build time.

check.q: When is the HTML for a static page generated?
check.a: At build time, before any visit
check.why: That is the definition of static rendering - the work is done once, ahead of time.

check.q: Which feature does a Next.js static export NOT support?
check.why: ISR needs a running server to regenerate pages, so it is on the unsupported list.

check.a: Client-side fetch or a deferred server island
